I actually used this last summer when I was helping my dad build a deck in our backyard. We needed to make sure the corners were perfectly square, so he had me measure out 3 feet on one side and 4 feet on the other, then check if the diagonal was 5 feet. It worked because 3² + 4² = 5² (9 + 16 = 25). It was kind of cool to see something I learned in class actually apply to real life instead of just being numbers on a worksheet.

**Prime factorization** means breaking down a composite number into a product of prime numbers only. For example, to factor 24: 24 = 2 × 12 = 2 × 2 × 6 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3, so 24 = 2³ × 3.

A helpful method is the **factor tree**: start with your number and split it into any two factors. Keep splitting composite factors until every branch ends in a prime number. Circle the primes and multiply them together for your answer.

Remember, prime numbers are only divisible by 1 and themselves (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13...). Practice with 36: you might split it into 4 × 9, then 2 × 2 and 3 × 3, giving you 36 = 2² × 3².

Decimals are a way to represent numbers less than one (or parts of a whole) using place value. The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts. Each position to the right of the decimal point represents a decreasing power of 10: tenths (0.1), hundredths (0.01), thousandths (0.001), and so on. For example, in 3.47, the 3 represents three wholes, the 4 represents four tenths, and the 7 represents seven hundredths. You can think of decimals as fractions with denominators of 10, 100, 1000, etc. Adding and subtracting decimals works just like whole numbers—just line up the decimal points. For multiplication, multiply normally and count total decimal places in the factors to place the decimal in the answer.
